# Results — Study 284 (Equinox-Effect) on the ^GSPC daily tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). Equinox/solstice
dates are hardcoded in [`data.py`](../equinox_effect/data.py) (computed from Meeus'
algorithm, 1928–2026). ^GSPC daily close-to-close price returns are from the
repo-level cache (`_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet`). Match the fingerprint below
to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n observations | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| ^GSPC daily (split-adjusted close, price-only) | 1928-01-03 – 2026-06-12 | 24,728 daily returns | `2fa7d20bebfd` |
| Equinox/solstice table | 1928–2026 (Meeus algorithm) | 396 events (393 in window) | hardcoded constant |

Survivorship note: ^GSPC is the index itself, so there is no constituent
survivorship bias — but it is **price-only** (no dividends) and the daily mean
drift is the honest baseline below.

## Event-study design

For each equinox/solstice, **event day 0** is the first ^GSPC trading day on/after
the astronomical instant (one built-in execution-lag day — the soonest a trader
could act). The **abnormal return** is the event-day return minus the full-sample
daily mean (`uncond = 3.15 bps/day`). We test the mean abnormal return with a
Newey-West (HAC, 3 lag) t-stat and a permutation test (10,000 random-day
resamples, same n).

## Headline: do equinoxes/solstices mark turning points?

| Slice | n | mean abnormal (bps) | HAC t | perm p |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| **All events** | 393 | **−3.0** | **−0.54** | **0.611** |
| Equinoxes only | 197 | −13.2 | −1.62 | 0.117 |
| Solstices only | 196 | +7.2 | +0.96 | 0.394 |
| Spring equinox | 99 | −4.9 | −0.46 | 0.684 |
| Summer solstice | 98 | +7.7 | +0.67 | 0.517 |
| Autumn equinox | 98 | **−21.6** | **−1.90** | **0.072** |
| Winter solstice | 98 | +6.7 | +0.74 | 0.573 |

- The headline (all 393 events) shows an abnormal return of **−3 bps** on the
  event trading day — a rounding error, and statistically a non-event: HAC t =
  **−0.54**, permutation p = **0.61**. The event-day win rate is **49.4%**, *below*
  the ~54% unconditional up-day rate — no turn, no swoon, no rally.
- No single season carries a significant effect. The autumn equinox is the most
  negative (−21.6 bps, HAC t = −1.90) — but that is just the historically weak
  **September seasonal** leaking in, and it falls **short of |t| = 2 even raw**.
- The 11-day CAR window (−5..+5) sums to **−19.6 bps**, statistically
  indistinguishable from a random 11-day drift around the event.

## The multiple-comparisons trap (why even the autumn slice is a mirage)

The **autumn-equinox** slice looks weakly interesting raw (perm p = 0.072, HAC t =
−1.90), but it never clears 0.05 in the first place, and we tested **seven** slices
on the same tape. Bonferroni-correcting for 7 simultaneous tests:

| Slice | perm p | Bonferroni perm p |
|---|--:|--:|
| all events | 0.611 | 1.00 |
| equinoxes only | 0.117 | 0.822 |
| solstices only | 0.394 | 1.00 |
| spring equinox | 0.684 | 1.00 |
| summer solstice | 0.517 | 1.00 |
| autumn equinox | 0.072 | **0.500** |
| winter solstice | 0.573 | 1.00 |

After correction nothing comes close to 0.05. The "autumn-equinox effect" is the
ordinary September weakness in disguise — there is no mechanism by which the Sun's
calendar (the Earth's axial tilt) would move US equities on a single day.

## The tiny-n / tiny-effect problem

With ~99 events per season and ~1% daily ^GSPC volatility, the standard error on a
seasonal event-day mean is roughly `1% / sqrt(99) ≈ 10 bps`, so a per-season
abnormal return must exceed ~20 bps consistently to clear |t| = 2. The autumn
slice (−22 bps) sits right at that edge — i.e. it is exactly the size of the
strongest random slice you would expect among seven tries.

## Positive control

On a synthetic daily tape with a planted event-day **drag** the engine recovers it
cleanly (n_permutations = 1,000, seed = 284):

| planted (bps) | recovered mean abn (bps) | HAC t | perm p |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | +4.3 | +0.88 | 0.393 |
| −50 | −45.0 | −9.3 | 0.000 |
| −150 | −143.4 | −29.7 | 0.000 |
| −300 | −291.1 | −60.2 | 0.000 |

The machinery detects a real effect when one exists; the real tape has nothing
like it.

## Could you trade it?

There is no tradable implementation. The signal fires four times a year, once per
equinox/solstice, for a single day. A long/flat or long/short "event-day" overlay
pays one-way costs on every turn (shorts also pay borrow), captures a noise-level
−3 bps gross, and is dominated by simply staying invested. Gross ≈ net only
because there is no edge to erode.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** All-event abnormal return −3 bps, HAC t = −0.54, perm p =
  0.61 — essentially zero. No slice survives multiple-comparisons correction; the
  most extreme (autumn equinox) is below |t| = 2 even before correction. n per
  season is too small to detect anything below ~20 bps.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** No vehicle: a four-times-a-year, single-day overlay
  with trading costs is dominated by passive buy-and-hold; there is no edge to
  monetise.
- **Busted — a turning point that isn't.** Markets have been said to "turn" with
  the Sun's calendar since the Gann era, but on 98 years of ^GSPC data the
  equinox/solstice trading day is indistinguishable from any other day.
